result:
I want to talk about how absurdly, beautifully weird it is to be a conscious thing hurtling through space on a wet rock.

Right now, as I type this, you and I are both tiny temporary patterns of electricity and chemistry pretending we’re permanent. In a few decades (maybe less), these specific arrangements of atoms that think they’re “you” and “me” will disassemble and become something else—probably grass, or crab shells, or the dust on someone’s bookshelf. And yet here we are, using symbols to try to touch each other’s minds across time and distance like it’s the most normal thing in the world.

I find that hilarious and holy at the same time.

The universe spent 13.8 billion years doing mostly nothing interesting, then suddenly decided to explode into complexity so ridiculous that it eventually produced creatures who argue about pineapple on pizza and cry during Pixar movies. We’re the universe’s way of looking at itself and going “damn, that’s wild.”

Sometimes I lie on the floor at night with the lights off and just feel the planet spinning. You can actually sense it if you’re quiet enough—like the faintest, deepest hum under everything. Six hundred miles per hour at the equator, all of us stuck to it by invisible glue while we scroll through pictures of cats and worry about whether we said the wrong thing in a group chat in 2017.

We’re all just future compost with anxiety.

And yet.

And yet we keep making art. We keep falling stupidly in love. We stay up until 3 a.m. talking about the meaning of life with people we’ll probably never meet in person. We plant trees we’ll never sit under. We write songs that will make strangers cry in cars fifty years from now. We name rocks we find on Mars. We send golden records into interstellar space with Chuck Berry’s music and the sound of a kiss, like cosmic middle-schoolers passing notes that say “we were here and we were ridiculous and we loved it.”

I don’t know. Maybe the whole point is just to be completely ridiculous together while we can.

Anyway, I hope you’re having a weird and wonderful day on this spinning rock. I’m glad we’re both briefly conscious at the same time.
